walkthroughs.body_html:
Some reactions go both ways.

The half-arrow symbol ⇌ means a reversible reaction. Reactants make products, and products can re-form reactants.

Example: ammonium chloride heats up to give ammonia + hydrogen chloride. Cool them and they recombine. NH₄Cl ⇌ NH₃ + HCl.

In a closed system, a reversible reaction reaches equilibrium. Both directions still happen, but at the same rate.

So the amounts of reactants and products don't change — even though particles keep reacting. That's why it's called dynamic.

It doesn't mean equal amounts of each. Just equal forward and backward speeds.

If you change the conditions, the equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.

Add more reactant? It shifts forward to use it up — more product made.

Remove product? It shifts forward to replace it.

The system always pushes back against whatever you do to it.

mcqs.q: Does a catalyst affect the position of equilibrium?
options: A catalyst shifts the equilibrium towards the products.
A catalyst increases the yield by being consumed in the forward reaction only.
No — it speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but at the same position.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.

mcqs.q: At dynamic equilibrium, what is happening to the reactions?
options: A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
Both reactions stop because the system has reached balance.
Forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; concentrations remain constant.
The forward reaction stops once the reverse reaction begins.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: A catalyst increases the yield by being consumed in the forward reaction only.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
